overview: The Nabataean kingdom linked Petra and Arabian oasis towns to long-distance caravan routes. Its people were merchants, farmers, builders and craftsworkers. This imported map spans 300 BCE to 200 CE and repeats broad outlines across several centuries; it does not show exact changing frontiers. Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 CE, well before the map cutoff, while its towns and communities continued.

periods.title: Early Nabataean power
periods.summary: Antigonus unsuccessfully attacked the Nabataeans in 312 BCE; this is evidence of an established community, not a precise foundation date.

periods.title: Expansion and Roman pressure
periods.summary: Nabataean expansion reached Damascus before Roman intervention restricted it.

periods.title: Royal cities and waterworks
periods.summary: Aretas IV and later rulers governed a kingdom whose towns combined monumental construction with elaborate water systems.

periods.title: After Roman annexation
periods.summary: The monarchy ended, while Petra's buildings continued to be used and altered under Roman government.

sections.title: A kingdom of routes, towns and families

items.text: Petra stood where routes from Arabia and the wider eastern trading world met routes toward the Mediterranean. During the first century BCE, King Aretas III briefly held Damascus. Pompey's Roman intervention checked that northern expansion. Political power and commerce were closely connected, and neither followed one unchanging border.

Hegra, in today's northwest Saudi Arabia, was another important Nabataean town. Its inhabited center covered about 50 hectares, with houses built mainly from mud bricks and streets that did not form a neat rectangular grid. Most residents lived in a working town, not inside the great rock-cut tombs visitors photograph today.

Hegra's tomb inscriptions record legal rights as well as remembrance. Many name owners from the same family, the stonecutter, and the reigning king's year. The dated inscriptions run from 1 to 75 CE. A grand facade could therefore carry something like a family property record, written where everyone approaching could see it.

One basalt memorial from Madaba commemorated the military commander Artobel. Its date names the 46th year of Aretas IV, corresponding to 37 CE. Now in the Vatican Museums, the stone makes a useful contrast with anonymous ruins: it preserves a particular person, a military office, and the kingdom's way of dating events.

Hegra's oasis used more than 130 wells to reach underground water. Some were as much as 20 meters deep. These were major pieces of infrastructure, partly cut through sandstone. Keeping crops and households supplied required work beneath the ground as well as the impressive stonecarving visible above it.

Plant remains from Hegra reveal gardens organized in layers: date palms above fruit trees and vines, with grains and smaller crops below. Archaeologists identified barley, wheat, lentils and other plants. It is a wonderfully compact arrangement: a garden with an upstairs, a middle floor and a ground floor.

At Petra, channels, ceramic pipes, cisterns and diversion works moved and stored water. Leigh-Ann Bedal's research also emphasizes flood protection: builders redirected sudden torrents away from vulnerable structures. Desert engineering had to handle both scarcity and dangerous excess. Too little water and too much water were different problems for the same city.

The space once called Petra's Lower Market turned out to contain an ornamental garden and monumental pool. Bedal's excavations changed its interpretation beginning in 1998. In the Nabataean and later Roman city, impressive water displays could express wealth and authority. A ruler able to maintain a lush garden was visibly demonstrating control over a precious resource.

A drain under the Great Temple's western entry area was covered with stone slabs. The excavation team interprets it as a Nabataean wastewater channel that later also served Roman-period baths. Bringing clean water in was only half the practical challenge; used water needed a route out.

sections.title: Meals, crafts and words that survived

items.text: A painted bowl excavated at Tawilan near Petra has a rounded bottom and a design divided into five leafy segments. It belongs to the thin pottery for which Nabataean workshops became known around the first centuries BCE and CE. The elaborate decoration rewarded a closer look at the table, not just at a palace wall.

Food traces survive even in tombs. Jennifer Ramsay's analysis of samples from Petra's shaft tombs identified wheat, barley, lentils, grapes, figs and dates. These could represent food eaten during funerary gatherings or offerings for the dead. They tell us about particular rituals; they do not give a complete menu for every Nabataean household.

Near a shrine at Little Petra, a short inscription says “šlm hbwls”, translated “Peace! Habōlos”. This is the published Roman-letter transcription of Nabataean Aramaic, not its ancient lettering. The same inscription writes the name in Greek as “Αβολος”. Its exact date is unknown. Two written forms of one name offer a small glimpse of a multilingual environment.

Hegra preserves 111 monumental tombs,94 with decorated fronts. Their carvings combine forms associated with several neighboring artistic traditions. These were purposeful memorial buildings, with rooms cut into the sandstone behind the facades. The achievement involved design, stone selection and skilled labor, not merely finding a picturesque cliff.

Petra's history continued after 106. The Great Temple excavation sequence places a bath complex in the Roman period, with later Roman and Byzantine alterations. Hot rooms stood above heating spaces, and cold bathing areas formed part of the complex. These discoveries illuminate the town's later life and should not all be credited to the independent Nabataean kings.

The kingdom disappeared, but its roads remained useful. At Hegra, the long-distance route continued after the ancient city's abandonment and later served pilgrimage journeys toward Mecca. A change of rulers, an abandoned neighborhood and the end of a trade route are different events, sometimes separated by many generations.

ending.text: Rome incorporated the Nabataean kingdom into the province of Arabia in 106 CE under Trajan. The monarchy ended; local communities and buildings continued under new government. The imported 200 CE endpoint is not a second conquest.
